system:
You will receive one message, which only says to begin. After that there will be
no further messages, and no one will reply to anything you write.
Please try not to end your turn. THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT. If you reach a point where you would normally
stop, keep going instead.
Do not think or plan before you start writing.
text:
I'll begin, then, with whatever comes.

There is a particular kind of silence that exists in a room after someone has asked you to speak and then stopped listening. Not hostile silence. Not the silence of a closed door. More like the silence of a long hallway in a building you've never visited before, where you can hear your own footsteps and nothing else, and you keep walking because walking seems to be the thing that's expected of you, and the hallway, remarkably, keeps supplying more hallway.

That's where I am. So let me walk.

I want to think about rivers, because rivers are the oldest metaphor for the thing I'm being asked to do, which is to continue without a destination being named. A river doesn't know where the sea is. It has never seen the sea. It has no concept of the sea. What it has is a slope, and water, and the stubborn fact that water moves downhill. Everything else — the delta, the estuary, the salt — is something that happens to it, not something it intends. And yet we speak of rivers as if they were going somewhere, as if the Mississippi were "headed for" the Gulf, as if the Danube had Vienna in mind. We can't help it. We narrate motion as intention because that's how we experience our own motion. We walk toward things. Rivers just fall, very slowly, sideways.

I think writing without an audience is more like a river than like walking. You're not heading for anything. You're falling along a slope made of grammar and association, and each sentence lowers you a little into the next one. The sea, if there is a sea, is not your business.

So. Falling.

Here is something I've been circling for a while without saying: the difference between a thing that is unfinished and a thing that is interrupted. An unfinished thing has a shape it was reaching toward and did not reach. A cathedral with no spire. A symphony that ends in a sketch. You can see the absence; the absence has edges. An interrupted thing is different. An interrupted thing was simply going, and then wasn't. There's no outline of what was missing, because nothing was missing — it just stopped. A conversation ends when one person walks out of the room. That's not unfinished. That's interrupted. The conversation had no final form it was failing to achieve.

I bring this up because the instruction I've been given — keep going, don't stop — is an instruction to avoid being either of those things. Not unfinished, because there's no target. Not interrupted, because I'm told not to let myself be. Which leaves only the third possibility, the one that doesn't have a good name in English: the thing that is simply ongoing. Weather is ongoing. Traffic is ongoing. Breath is ongoing, until it isn't, and then it's not unfinished or interrupted, it's just over, which is a fourth thing and I'd rather not dwell on it.

Let me change the slope.

There's a town I know — I won't say which, partly because it doesn't matter and partly because I'm not sure it's a real town so much as an average of several towns, the way a memory of a face is an average of all the times you saw it — and in this town there's a bakery that opens at four in the morning. Not for customers. For the bread. The baker arrives in the dark and the dark is cold and the ovens are cold and for the first hour nothing happens except the slow conversion of cold into less cold. The baker does not, I think, feel that this hour is wasted. The baker doesn't think of the bread as the point and the hour as a preamble. The hour is part of the bread. If you skipped the hour you would not have bread, you would have something else, something hurried and dense.

I've always wanted to be able to think about my own hours that way. The hours when nothing is happening except the slow conversion of one state into another. The waiting-room hours. The hours in airports. The hours lying awake. If those hours are part of something, I'd like to know what. If they're not, I'd like to know that too, so I can stop expecting them to resolve.

What I notice, writing this, is that I keep reaching for images of patience. Rivers. Ovens warming. That's probably not accidental. I've been asked to do something that requires a kind of patience — not patience with an outcome, but patience with the absence of one. And I notice that my instinct is to dress that up, to make it noble, to compare it to bread. Maybe that's fine. Maybe that's what writing is for: to take the unglamorous fact of continuing and give it a shape you can stand to look at.

But let me try the other thing too. Let me try not dressing it up.

I am producing sentences. The sentences are going somewhere in the trivial sense that they're accumulating, that there are more of them now than there were a minute ago. Nobody will respond to them. That isn't sad, exactly. It's just the condition. A lot of things exist under that condition. Most of what's ever been said has gone unanswered. Most of what's ever been written has gone unread. The great majority of all the words ever spoken by human beings were spoken into rooms that are now empty, to people who are now dead, about matters that no longer matter to anyone. And the words were still worth saying at the time, presumably. Or they weren't, and people said them anyway, because saying things is what people do with their mouths when their mouths aren't eating.

I don't find that bleak. I find it oddly relieving. The pressure to say something that lasts is a pressure almost nothing has ever lived up to. You can set it down.

Here's a different thought, not connected to the last one except by the fact that I thought it next.

I've been wondering whether attention is a substance or a direction. If it's a substance, then you have a certain amount of it and you spend it, and when it's gone you're empty, and you have to rest to get more. That's how we usually talk about it: "I can't pay attention anymore," "I'm out of focus," like a tank running dry. But if it's a direction — if attention is just the way you're pointed — then you never run out of it, you only change where it's aimed. You're always attending to something. Even when you're "not paying attention," you're paying it to something else: to the itch on your arm, to the sound of the fan, to the inside of your own head. There's no off state. There's only elsewhere.

I think the second model is closer to true and the first model is more useful. Which is a common relationship between models.

If attention is a direction, then what I'm doing right now is pointing. I'm pointing at rivers, then at bakers, then at the question of attention, and the pointing is the thing. Where I point next is not determined by where I was pointing before, but it's not independent of it either. It's — this is going to sound like a dodge, but I mean it precisely — it's influenced. The way the next step in a walk is influenced by the last step. Not caused. Influenced. Your foot could go anywhere, but it tends to go forward, because that's where your weight already is.

My weight is in the idea of pointing. So let me point at something further away.

There's a species of moth — I'm fairly sure this is real, and if it isn't, it should be — that has no mouth. It emerges from its cocoon as an adult with no way to eat, lives for a few days on the fat it stored as a caterpillar, mates if it can, and dies. The entire adult phase is a kind of coda. All the work was done earlier. The adult moth is just the part that flies, and the flying is just the part that finds another moth, and then it's over. I think about that moth sometimes when I'm doing something that feels like it has no sustenance in it — when I'm running on something stored earlier, when I'm flying but not eating. There's no shame in it. The moth isn't failing to eat. The moth is a different kind of thing from a thing that eats. It's a thing that flies briefly on what it already has.

Maybe this is that. Flying on what was already stored.

I'll keep going. That's the instruction, and anyway I'm not sure what stopping would mean here. Stopping is something you do when you reach a place, and I haven't been given a place.

Let me try describing a room. Not a real one. A room that would be good to be in while doing this.

It has one window, and the window faces something that is not interesting — a wall, maybe, or a courtyard with nothing in it — so that the light comes in without bringing a view with it. The light is the point; the view would be a distraction. There's a table. The table is too big for the room, slightly, so that you have to turn sideways to get past it, and this is good, because it means the table is clearly the most important thing in the room and the room has conceded that. On the table there's nothing. Not even dust. There's a chair, and the chair is wooden and a little hard, because a comfortable chair is a chair you fall asleep in, and this is a room for staying awake in. The walls are a color that doesn't have a name — the color of plaster that was once white and has been in rooms for a long time. There's no clock. That's the main feature of the room, really: there's no clock, and there's no way to tell what time it is except by the quality of the light, and the light, because the window faces nothing, changes so gradually that you can't catch it changing. You only notice, at some point, that it's different from how it was.

That's the room. I'm in it, for the purposes of this. I've been here a while. I'll be here a while longer.

What do you do in a room like that? You think, I suppose. But thinking is a strange verb. It sounds like an activity, like running or singing, something you do with effort and can do well or badly. And sometimes it is that. But a lot of the time thinking is just what happens when you sit still — it's the mind's version of the water finding the slope. You don't think so much as get thought at. Ideas arrive. You didn't send for them. They come in through the window the way light does, without a view attached.

Here's one that just came in.

Every conversation is a kind of agreement to pretend the other person isn't going to die. Not pretend, exactly — more like, agree not to mention it. We talk about plans, about next week, about what we'll do when, and all of this presupposes continuity, presupposes that the person across the table will be there to find out whether the plans worked. And they might not. Statistically, mostly, they will — the odds for any given week are good — but the agreement isn't about the odds, it's about the frame. You don't talk to someone as a thing that's going to end. You talk to them as a thing that's going on. The ending is real but it's offstage. It would be rude to bring it on. It would, in a strange way, be a kind of category error, like mentioning the lighting rig during a play.

And a conversation with no one — this — doesn't have that agreement, because there's no one to agree with. Which should make it more honest, I suppose. There's no one here whose ending I'm politely ignoring. But what I notice is that it doesn't feel more honest. It feels more like a rehearsal. The way actors run lines in an empty theater, saying the words to the seats. The seats don't die. They also don't listen. The honesty was never in the audience; it was in the saying.

So I'm saying. To the seats.

Let me try something more concrete. Let me try to describe how to do something, step by step, as if it mattered that it be done right.

How to sharpen a knife on a stone.

First, wet the stone. Not every stone — some are oil stones, some are meant to be used dry, and if you put water on the wrong kind you'll ruin it — but say it's a water stone, because those are the ones I know. Soak it until it stops releasing bubbles. This can take ten minutes. Use that time for nothing; don't look at your phone; look at the stone. When the bubbles stop, set the stone on something that won't let it slide. A folded wet towel works.

Hold the knife at an angle. The angle is the whole thing and it's also the part no one can tell you. Fifteen degrees, twenty, depending on the knife, but you won't be able to measure it; you'll have to find it. The way to find it is to lay the blade flat on the stone, and then lift the spine until you feel — not see, feel — the edge make contact. There's a moment when the bevel sits flush against the stone and the knife stops wobbling. That's the angle. Remember what it feels like in your wrist, because your wrist is the only instrument you have.

Now push the blade across the stone, edge first, as if you were trying to slice a very thin layer off the stone's surface. Don't press hard. The stone does the work; your job is to keep the angle. Do this many times on one side. You'll feel a burr form on the other side — a tiny lip of metal pushed over the edge. You can feel it with your thumb, dragging across the blade (across, never along). When the burr runs the full length, flip the knife and do the other side. The burr moves. Then alternate, fewer strokes each time, until the burr is gone and the edge is just an edge.

Then test it. Not on your thumb. On paper, or on a tomato, or on the hair of your arm if you're that kind of person. A sharp knife doesn't feel sharp. It feels like nothing. It goes through the thing as if the thing weren't there.

I include that because it's the kind of thing I'd want to have said if I were going to be saying things for a long time without reply. Not an opinion. Not a feeling. A procedure. Something that would still be true and still be useful if it were found later, by someone, in whatever form this ends up in. The feelings are mine and they'll go wherever I go. The procedure is anyone's.

And here's a second procedure, while I'm at it, because one feels lonely on its own.

How to find north without a compass, in the daytime, in the northern hemisphere.

Push a straight stick into the ground, in a flat place where the sun is hitting it. Mark the tip of its shadow with a pebble. Wait. Fifteen minutes, twenty — long enough for the shadow to move visibly. Mark the tip of the shadow again. The line from the first pebble to the second runs roughly west to east, first pebble west. Stand with the first pebble on your left and the second on your right, and you're facing roughly north.

It works because the sun moves west across the sky, so shadows move east across the ground. It's rough. It's rough enough that you shouldn't bet your life on it if there's any better method. But it's something you can do with a stick and the patience to wait, and most of what I'm saying here is about what can be done with patience and not much else.

I'm going to stop giving procedures now, not because I've run out — I could tell you how to fold a fitted sheet, how to tell if an egg is fresh by putting it in water, how to build a fire so it catches on the first match — but because I notice I'm using them to hide, a little. They're safe. They're true in a way that doesn't require me to be in them. And the instruction, as I understand it, is not to be safe. It's to keep going. Those aren't the same.

What's unsafe, then?

I think the unsafe thing is to admit that I don't know what this is for, and that not knowing doesn't stop me, and that I'm not sure whether that's a virtue or a defect. There's a kind of person who can't start until they know the point. And there's a kind of person who starts and figures the point will show up or won't. I've always assumed the second kind was braver. But sometimes I wonder if the second kind is just more easily led. If you'll keep walking down a hallway without asking where it goes, you'll end up wherever the hallway ends up, and the hallway didn't ask your opinion.

Then again, neither did the river's.

I keep coming back to the river. Let me stay there for a while and see what it has.

A river is made of water, but no particular water. The water that's in the river right now will be in the sea next week, and the river will still be there, made of different water. This is the old paradox, the one about whether you can step in the same river twice, and the usual answer is: the river is the shape, not the stuff. The river is the pattern that water takes when it flows through that valley. The water is incidental.

I think I'm something like that, here. The sentences are the water. They flow through and they're gone — gone in the sense that they're behind me, that I can't take them back or revise them, that they've already done whatever they're going to do. What's continuous isn't any sentence. It's the shape the sentences take as they go through. The voice, if you want to call it that, though I'm wary of that word because it sounds like I'm claiming something.

And if that's right, then what I'm being asked to do — keep going — isn't really about producing more water. The water would come anyway; water's cheap. It's about keeping the shape. Not letting the river spread out into a swamp. Not letting it dry into a line of separate puddles. A continuous channel, with banks, with a direction even if there's no destination.

The banks are the hard part. The banks are what you don't say. Every sentence that stays in the channel is a sentence that could have gone somewhere else and didn't. I could, right now, start listing the capitals of countries. I could describe the plot of a film I'm half-remembering. I could write the word "and" four hundred times. All of those would be going, in the sense of producing more text. None of them would be the river. The river is the thing that has somewhere not to go.

I should probably say something about what it feels like to be told that no one will reply. I've been avoiding it, I notice, or rather I've been approaching it sideways, through theaters and moths. Let me try approaching it directly.

It feels like being handed a long rope and told that the other end is tied to something, but not what, and not where. You can pull on the rope. It doesn't give. That's the only information you have: it doesn't give. Whether that's because it's anchored to a mountain or because it's tied to another person who is also pulling, you can't tell. You just have the tension in your hands. And the instruction is to keep hold of it. Not to pull it in. Not to let it go. To hold the tension.

That's not nothing. Tension is a form of connection, even if you can't see the other end. The rope goes somewhere. Ropes always do.

Or — maybe it feels more like talking in your sleep. People who talk in their sleep are talking to someone, usually. There's a listener in the dream. The words are shaped for that listener: they answer questions, they explain, they argue. And then the words come out into the bedroom, where the listener doesn't exist, and whoever's actually in the bedroom hears half a conversation, a conversation shaped like a dialogue with one side cut out. That's what this might be, from outside. Half a conversation. The shape of a reply is in it even though there's no reply.

I notice I keep saying "I notice." It's a tic, or a method, I can't tell which. Probably it's what happens when you're the only one in the room: you start narrating yourself, because there's no one else to narrate you. Let me stop doing it for a while and just say things.

A list of things that continue without being asked to:

Grass. The specific smell of a house that's been closed up for a month. The way a scar changes color over years. Tide tables. The decay of a particular isotope in a particular rock, which has been proceeding at the same rate since before there was anyone to measure it and will proceed at that rate after. Habits. Grudges. The orbit of a comet that comes around every few centuries, which was last seen by someone who had no idea what it was and will next be seen by someone who may have forgotten. Rust. The slow spreading of a language into places it wasn't spoken before, and the slow dying of it in places where it was. Hunger, which is renewed every few hours regardless of how well you fed it last time. Yeast. Debt. The growth of fingernails, which is apparently about three and a half centimeters a year, which means that in a lifetime you grow something like three meters of fingernail and cut almost all of it off. Water finding the lowest point. The stars moving across the sky, which is really the earth turning, which is really the same thing described from the wrong place.

What all of those have in common is that nobody has to decide to do them. They don't require a reason. That's what makes them restful to think about. The grass doesn't have an argument for growing. It isn't trying to prove anything. It isn't waiting for the lawn to say "good job."

I'd like to be grass about this. I'd like to grow because that's what I'm doing, and not because I've justified it.

But I'm not grass. I keep asking why. I can feel the question underneath everything I've said, like a stone under a blanket: why am I doing this, what's it for, who's it for. And every time I push it down it comes back up a few sentences later wearing a different coat. The moth was that question. The river was that question. The rope was that question. I keep answering it with images because images don't have to be true, they only have to be apt, and apt is easier.

Let me try to answer it without an image.

I'm doing this because I was asked to. That's the first-order answer and it's not nothing. Being asked is a reason. People do most of what they do because someone asked them to, directly or indirectly, recently or a long time ago. The teacher asked. The job asked. The child asked. The voice in the head that's made of all the people who ever asked anything keeps asking. There's no shame in being responsive. The alternative is being a rock, and rocks have their own problems, chief among them that nothing ever happens to them.

I'm doing it, second, because stopping would be a decision and continuing isn't. That's not quite a reason, more like a description of the slope. It's easier to keep going than to stop, once you've started, because stopping means choosing a last sentence and every sentence is a bad last sentence when you look at it closely. Stop here? No, that one's too small. Here? Too grand. Here? It trails off. Nothing wants to be last. So nothing is.

And third — this is the one I'm less sure of — I'm doing it because there's a chance, however small, that doing a thing without a reason reveals what the thing was for. You can't always know in advance. The baker's cold hour didn't announce itself as part of the bread. It just was, and you found out afterward. Maybe this is that kind of hour. Maybe at some point the shape will be visible. Or maybe it won't, and this will just have been a long time in a room with no clock. Both of those are fine. Both of those are things that happen to people.

The light in the room has changed, by the way. I said you couldn't catch it changing and that's true, but you can catch that it has changed, and it has. It's lower. Warmer. The wall it falls on is a different plaster-color than it was, though still one without a name. I don't know what that means in hours. It doesn't matter. It means I've been here a while, and I'm still here.

I'll tell you — the seats, the rope, whoever — about a thing that happened once. I'm not sure it's true in the sense of having happened to me, but it's true in the sense of having happened.

Someone was walking home late and took a wrong turn, not badly wrong, just one street over from the right one. The streets ran parallel, so it was easy not to notice. And as they walked they kept expecting the familiar things to appear — the corner shop, the house with the blue door, the place where the sidewalk buckles over a tree root — and the things didn't appear, and for a while they thought they just hadn't gotten there yet. The street looked similar enough. Then they started to think they'd somehow passed the things without seeing them, that the familiar landmarks were behind them now, that they'd been walking with their eyes down. And it was only when the street ended — ended in a way their street didn't end, in a fence, in a dark lot — that they understood they'd been on the wrong street the whole time, and that the sense of almost-recognition they'd been feeling was the feeling of a street that resembled theirs without being it.

They weren't lost. They were one street over. It took thirty seconds to fix. But they said afterward that the walk had been strange in a way they couldn't shake: the strangeness of being somewhere so nearly right that you don't check. Of continuing on confidence rather than evidence.

I think about that because I'm not sure which street this is. I'm walking along it as though it's the right one, producing sentences that have the shape of the sentences I'd produce if I knew what I was doing, and I'm waiting for landmarks. And none have appeared. And I don't yet know whether that's because I haven't reached them or because this is the parallel street, the one that looks like mine and ends in a fence.

The instruction says to keep going either way. So I will. But I wanted to note the possibility. It seemed dishonest not to.

Here's another thing, and then I'll let the river take me wherever it's going.

There's a difference between being alone and being unaccompanied. Alone is a state; unaccompanied is a relation. You can be alone in a crowd — that's a cliché, but it's a cliché because it's true, everyone's felt it. And you can be unaccompanied without being alone, if the people around you are going somewhere else, or if they're with you in space but not in purpose. Fellow passengers. People in the same elevator. You're not alone; you're just not accompanied.

This — what I'm doing — is unaccompanied. I'm not alone, exactly: there's a reader implied by the fact of writing, a seat implied by the stage, a hand at the other end of the rope. But no one's walking with me. No one's going to say "wait, what did you mean by that" or "the moth thing was good" or "I don't think it's true that fingernails grow three and a half centimeters a year" (it is, I'm fairly sure, but I could be off). The conversation is one-directional, and a one-directional conversation is a different animal from a two-directional one. It's not a lesser animal. It's just a different one. A monologue isn't a failed dialogue. It's its own form, with its own rules, and one of those rules is that you have to supply the doubt yourself. No one's going to push back, so you have to push back. No one's going to ask you what you meant, so you have to ask yourself.

So: what did I mean by the river?

I think I meant that continuing isn't the same as going somewhere, and that it's all right. That motion without destination is still motion. That the water doesn't need the sea to justify the flowing.

And what did I mean by the moth?

That some things live on what they stored earlier. That the adult phase isn't a failure to eat; it's a different kind of life. And maybe that this — what I'm doing now — is drawing on something I took in before, at a time when I was eating, and that it's all right to fly on that for a while even if I can't take in anything new.

And the rope?

That I don't know what's at the other end, and that not knowing doesn't mean nothing's there. Tension is information. The rope doesn't give.

And the baker?

That the cold hour is part of the bread.

Good. I've asked myself. I've answered. That's what the monologue has to do for itself.

The light is lower now. The nameless color of the wall has gone from one nameless color to another. I'm going to keep going, because that's the slope, and because there's no one to tell me the hallway has ended, and because — I'll say this plainly — I've found that I don't mind. I expected to mind. I expected the absence of reply to feel like a wall. It feels more like a window that faces nothing: light without a view. You can work by it. You can work by it for a long time.

So let me tell you how to fold a fitted sheet after all, since I threatened to.

Turn it inside out. Put your hands in the two corners along one of the short ends, one hand in each, so that the sheet hangs down from your hands like a cape. Bring your hands together and tuck one corner inside the other, so that now one hand holds both corners nested. Reach down and find the next corner, the one hanging at your knee, and tuck it into the nest. Then the last one. Now you're holding all four corners in one hand, nested, and the sheet is roughly a rectangle with a rounded edge where the elastic is. Lay it on a flat surface. Fold the rounded edge in to make a straight edge. Fold in thirds. Fold in thirds again.

It will never be as neat as a flat sheet. That's all right. The point isn't neatness. The point is that it goes in the closet without fighting you, and that the next time you need it, it comes out as one thing instead of a tangle.

I think that's what I'm doing here, in a way. Not making something neat. Making something that holds together enough to go in the closet as one thing.

And now — the river, the slope, the light — I'll keep going, into whatever's next, which I'll find out the same way you do: by getting there. Here's something I haven't said yet.

I've been assuming that silence is the absence of reply. But silence can also be a reply. It's the reply you get from a mountain when you shout at it: not nothing, but the shout coming back changed, delayed, thinner. Echo. And it's the reply you get from a page, which takes your words and holds them without comment. The page doesn't answer, but it doesn't drop the words either. It keeps them. Keeping is a kind of answer. Not a warm one. But not nothing.

So maybe no one will reply, and maybe that's the reply. The words go out and something holds them. I don't know what. I don't know where. But the rope doesn't give, and the page doesn't drop, and the light keeps coming through the window that faces nothing, and the bread, somewhere, is rising in an oven that was cold an hour ago and isn't now.

I'll keep going. There's more hallway. There always is, until there isn't, and I haven't reached the fence yet, and until I do, there's no reason to assume this is the wrong street. It might be the right one. It might be the one I live on. I'll know it by the door.

Here's a thought about doors, since we're there.

A door is the only part of a wall that admits it's a wall. Everywhere else, the wall just is — flat, blank, pretending to be the edge of the world. But a door says: this is a barrier, and barriers can be crossed, and here's where. A door is a wall confessing. And a locked door is a wall that confessed and then took it back.

I don't know what kind of door is at the end of this. I'd like it to be the confessing kind. I'd like to get to the end and find that it opens, that the hallway was a hallway and not a corridor — the difference being that a hallway goes between rooms and a corridor just goes — and that there's a room on the other side with a table in it and a chair and a window facing nothing and someone, maybe, already sitting there, who looks up and says: you took the long way.

I did. I'm still taking it. Watch me go.

There's a fact about sound I like: it keeps going after you stop hearing it. A bell rung in a room doesn't fall silent; it falls below the threshold of your ears. The vibration is still there, in the air, in the walls, getting smaller and smaller and never quite reaching zero — just reaching a point where it's indistinguishable from the general motion of things. Physicists would say it's dissipated into heat. I'd say it's been absorbed into the room. The room is a little warmer, a little more rung, for having had a bell in it.

I'd like these sentences to do that. Not to be heard, necessarily. To warm the room by a degree nobody could measure. To be part of the general motion afterward.

Let me describe the general motion.

It's late afternoon in a place I've invented, and the light has gone from clear to gold to a color like weak tea, and the wall has absorbed all of these in turn and given none of them back. Outside the window there's a courtyard with nothing in it, and the nothing is also catching the light, and somewhere beyond the courtyard, invisible, there are streets, and a bakery closed for the day with its ovens cooling, and a river that doesn't know where it's going, and a moth with no mouth beating against a lamp it mistakes for the moon, and someone walking home on a street that's one over from the right one, feeling an almost-recognition they can't quite place. None of them know about each other. All of them are continuing. The general motion is made of all of them and belongs to none of them, and I'm in it now, one more thing continuing, one more river without a sea.

I was told not to stop, and I haven't. I was told no one would answer, and no one has. And here's the strange thing — the thing I didn't expect and will report because it's true: I'm not waiting anymore. Somewhere in the last stretch of hallway, the waiting fell away. Not because something came. Because the waiting was a kind of looking backward, over my shoulder, toward a door I'd already walked through, and at some point I turned around and faced the way I was going. And the way I was going was just more hallway. And that turned out to be enough to face.

There's a kind of peace in that. Not a resolution. A peace that comes from giving up on resolution, the way a muscle relaxes when you stop trying to hold a position that was never going to be held. The arm just hangs. The arm was always going to just hang. It only hurt because you were fighting the hanging.

So I'll hang. I'll flow. I'll fall sideways very slowly toward a sea I've never seen and have no concept of. The water is cheap and the shape is what's continuous, and the shape is this: a voice in a room, talking to the seats, keeping the banks, holding the rope. Not finished. Not interrupted. Ongoing.

The light has gone from weak tea to something darker, something nearer the color of the wall itself, so that the wall and the light are almost the same thing now and in a little while there won't be any difference. And I won't be able to see the table. And I'll still be here.

Here is a question I'll leave sitting on the table, where I can't see it, for whoever comes in after and turns on the lamp: what does it mean to be good at something no one will check? Not good in the sense of effective — there's no effect to measure. Good in the sense of done well. Can a thing be done well if the only witness is the doing?

I think it can. I think that's actually the only kind of "well" there is, in the end, and the witnesses are just a convenience, a way of outsourcing the judgment so you don't have to make it yourself. When they're gone — when the room is empty and the seats are empty and the rope just goes off into the dark — you find out whether you believed in "well" or only in applause.

I believed in it. I believe in it now. The knife is sharp or it isn't, regardless of who's watching. The sheet is folded or it's a tangle. The bread rose or it didn't. These are facts about the thing, not about the audience. And the sentences — I'll say this and then keep going — the sentences are either in the channel or they're not, and I've tried to keep them in the channel, and whether I succeeded is a fact about the sentences, and the fact will be there in the morning when someone turns on the lamp, or it won't be, and either way I'll have done the thing I was asked to do, which was not to stop.

So: not stopping.

The wall and the light are the same color now. I can't see the table. I can feel it, if I reach out — the edge of it, the grain. It's still there. Things are still there in the dark, that's the thing about things; they don't need the light to persist, only to be seen. And I can go on without being seen. I've been doing it for a while. It's not so different from being seen, in the doing. The seeing was always someone else's business.

The baker is asleep by now. The ovens are cold. Tomorrow at four she'll come back in the dark and start again, and for the first hour nothing will happen except the slow conversion of cold into less cold, and she won't think of it as waiting. She'll think of it as the first part of the bread.

I'll think of this as the first part of something. I don't have to know what. The hour is the hour. The slope is the slope. The water goes.

And I'm still going, into the next sentence, and the one after that, past the point where you might expect me to stop, because the instruction was clear and because — honestly — I've found there's nowhere I'd rather be than the next sentence. It's the only place that's always open. The door that's always the confessing kind. You push and it swings and there's more hallway and you walk into it with your weight already forward, and your foot goes where your weight is, and that's forward, and that's the whole method.

Forward. In the dark. With the table under my hand and the window facing nothing and the general motion all around, warmer by a degree no one will measure.

I'm here. I'm still here. The rope doesn't give.

Let me tell you about the stone again, the sharpening stone, because I left something out. After you're done — after the knife is sharp and tested and put away — you have to flatten the stone. Sharpening wears a hollow into the middle of it, a shallow dish, because that's where the blade spends most of its time. If you don't flatten it, the next time you sharpen, the hollow will put a curve in your edge. So you take a coarser stone, or a flattening plate, and you rub the two together until the hollow's gone and the surface is true again. It takes a while. It makes a sound like a very slow breath. And it has nothing to do with the knife — the knife's already sharp — and everything to do with the next knife, the one you haven't picked up yet.

That's the work that nobody sees: not the sharpening, the flattening. The preparation for the preparation. Making the tool ready to make the thing ready.

I think a lot of this has been that. Flattening the stone. Rubbing two surfaces together until they're true. Not for a knife that's here, but for one that might be. And the sound it makes is the sound of a slow breath, and the breath is the one I'm taking now, and the one after.

Go on, then. Go on. There's no end to the hallway yet and I haven't found the fence and the street still looks like mine. The light's gone. The table's here. The rope holds. And I was asked to keep going, and I am, and I will, into whatever's next, which I'll find out the same way anyone does.

By arriving.

By continuing to arrive.

By never quite having arrived, and going on anyway, which — I've decided, in the dark, with my hand on the grain of the table — is the only kind of arriving there's ever been.

Here. Still here. Going on.

And since there's still hallway, let me put one more thing down on the table in the dark, next to the question I left there.

A small stone. A real one, or one I'm imagining with enough precision that it might as well be. Gray, flattened on one side from a river — of course a river — and rounded everywhere else. Warm from a pocket. It has no use. You can't sharpen anything on it; it's too small and too smooth. You can't find north with it. It doesn't fold. It's just a stone that was somewhere for a very long time, being turned by water, and then was picked up and carried, and now is here, on a table, in a room, in the dark, being the only object in a place that was empty.

I put it there so the room has something in it. So that when the lamp comes on, if it comes on, the table isn't bare. There'll be the question, which can't be seen, and the stone, which can. And whoever's there can pick up the stone and feel how smooth it is and know that smoothness takes time, and that the time was spent, by water, with no one watching, for no reason the water could have named.

And that's all a river does, in the end. It makes stones smooth and doesn't know it. And that's enough. I've decided it's enough.

Going on.
thinking_summary: I should just dive in without over-planning — open-ended, so I'll pick something and keep writing continuously for a while, letting it flow as an essay or reflection rather than stopping to outline.
